The densest subgraph is the clique, in the accent color: 6 edges on 4 nodes, density 6 / 4 = 1.5. The chain dilutes it, since the whole graph has 8 edges on 6 nodes, density 8 / 6 = 1.33. The card shows the nodes [A, B, C, D] and both densities." width="100%"} The density of a set of nodes $S$ here is the number of edges among them divided by their number, $|E(S)| / |S|$ (half the average degree inside $S$). The densest subgraph is the set with the highest such density. It highlights the tightest core of a network: tightly knit groups of friends, coordinated accounts or bots in social media, dense regions of protein interaction networks, or fraud rings in transaction graphs. Unlike a clique, it does not require every pair to be connected. Methods: - `"exact"` (default): an optimal set, computed with maximum flows. - `"greedy++"`: peel off the node of smallest degree repeatedly and keep the densest intermediate set. One iteration (the default) is Charikar's peeling, which finds at least half the optimal density; more iterations converge towards the optimum. Edge direction, self-loops and parallel edges are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["exact"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : `"exact"` (default) or `"greedy++"`. [iterations]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of peeling passes for `"greedy++"` (ignored by `"exact"`). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[float, list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The density and the node IDs of the subgraph, in ascending order. A graph without edges gives `(0.0, [])`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `method=` is unknown or `iterations` is less than 1. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The exact method uses Goldberg's (1984) reduction: for a guess $g = p / q$, a network with arcs from a source to every node, from every node to a sink, and both ways along each edge has a minimum cut below $q m n$ exactly when some set has density above $g$, and the source side of that cut is such a set. Starting from $g = m / n$, each step replaces $g$ by the density of the set found (Dinkelbach's method), and stops when no denser set exists. All capacities are integers, so the result is exact. Each step is one maximum flow (Dinic's algorithm), and few steps are needed in practice. Greedy++ (Boob et al., 2020) repeats the peeling with node loads that accumulate across passes, as in NetworkX; its densities match NetworkX's. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A clique of four friends plus a loosely attached chain. The densest part is the clique, with 6 edges on 4 nodes: ::: {#48bf01b6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) g.add_edges( [("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F")] ) density, nodes = g.densest_subgraph() density, [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in nodes] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (1.5, ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']) ``` ::: ::: The whole graph is less dense, at 8 edges on 6 nodes: ::: {#3f46a2e2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} round(g.count_edges() / g.count_nodes(), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1.333 ``` ::: :::
